justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a baseline around 413–414 for the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or a similar broad equity index. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, adding only a small expected drift since daily returns are nearly unpredictable and the best guess is essentially the current level plus a tiny risk premium. For the 1-week estimate, I nudged the forecast slightly higher to reflect the historical tendency for equities to drift upward over time, while acknowledging that a week is still short enough that momentum and near-term sentiment dominate. For the 1-month estimate, I extended that drift assumption further, arriving at roughly a 1.5–2% expected gain, which is consistent with annualized equity returns of around 8–10% prorated over a single month.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized volatility assumptions. At the 1-day horizon, I used something close to typical daily SPY volatility of around 1–1.5%, which yields a relatively tight band. As the horizon extends to a week, volatility scales with the square root of time, so the interval widens proportionally. By one month, uncertainty compounds further, and I also incorporated the possibility of regime changes — for instance, a shift in Federal Reserve tone, an unexpected inflation print, or geopolitical developments — which adds fat-tail risk beyond what pure statistical scaling would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals on the downside. A surprise in macroeconomic data — particularly a hotter-than-expected CPI report or a sharp deterioration in labor markets — could shift rate expectations dramatically and trigger a swift correction of 5% or more, which would breach the lower bound of my 1-month interval. Geopolitical escalation, a credit event in financial markets, or sudden liquidity stress could also produce outsized moves. On the upside, a dovish pivot from the Fed, stronger-than-expected earnings, or a resolution of trade or geopolitical tensions could push prices well above my upper bounds, particularly at the 1-month horizon.

It's worth noting that my intervals, while wide by everyday standards, are still based on relatively well-behaved volatility assumptions. In practice, equity markets occasionally experience tail events — flash crashes, policy surprises, or contagion from global markets — that fall in the 1–5% probability space but sit entirely outside a 90% confidence interval. These black-swan-style events are the hardest to incorporate into any forecast and represent the primary reason real-world outcomes can surprise even well-calibrated probabilistic models.
